adapter.scenario: Checkout expects pay(amount), but a legacy SDK exposes charge(cents).
adapter.request: Reuse the legacy SDK while the app keeps amounts in major units.
adapter.problem: Names and units differ. Editing every caller leaks SDK details into business code.
adapter.solution: Implement pay in an adapter, convert major units to cents and delegate to the SDK. The adapter changes the interface, not the business responsibility. Production money needs exact arithmetic and rounding policies.
adapter.when: Use it for an unmodifiable component with matching behavior but an incompatible interface.
adapter.avoid: Do not disguise different semantics by renaming methods. Align editable interfaces directly.
adapter.tradeoff: An extra delegation layer requires tests for units, errors and formats.
adapter.remember: Translate at the boundary while both sides retain their interfaces.

bridge.scenario: Messages have normal and urgent forms, with email and SMS delivery.
bridge.request: Add urgent messages while retaining both channels.
bridge.problem: A class per message/channel combination multiplies types and duplicates combinations.
bridge.solution: A message abstraction holds a sender interface. Normal and urgent messages shape content; email and SMS senders handle delivery. Composition connects the hierarchies so each dimension evolves independently.
benefits: Avoid multiplying classes for every combination.
bridge.when: Use it for two genuinely independent dimensions, such as message form and transport.
bridge.avoid: With one varying dimension, a simple interface or strategy is enough.
bridge.tradeoff: The bridge interface must be stable; poor boundaries leak details between hierarchies.
bridge.remember: Let two dimensions grow independently and connect them through composition.

composite.scenario: A basket contains individual items and bundles of items.
composite.request: Nest a bundle inside another bundle and calculate the total uniformly.
composite.problem: The caller distinguishes leaves from containers and handwrites loops for each nesting level.
composite.solution: Items and bundles share total. An item returns its price; a bundle recursively sums its children's totals. A tree exposes parts and wholes through the same operation.
benefits: Operate on leaves and composites uniformly.
Add nesting without changing the caller.
composite.when: Use it for natural part/whole trees such as menus, directories and component hierarchies.
composite.avoid: Cycles or shared graph nodes need more than tree recursion. Avoid forcing unrelated leaf and container responsibilities together.
composite.tradeoff: A uniform interface may hide important distinctions. Validate children and prevent cycles.
composite.remember: One item and a whole bundle both expose one total operation.

composite.distinction: Composite organizes a tree; Decorator typically builds a wrapper chain. Cyclic graphs need additional traversal policies.

decorator.scenario: Coffee has a base price and optional milk or sugar.
decorator.request: Combine milk and sugar, with more toppings to follow.
decorator.problem: Subclassing every topping combination explodes the type count. Putting every option in the base class keeps expanding its responsibility.
decorator.solution: Coffee and decorators share cost. Each decorator wraps a coffee, delegates to it and adds its own price. Layer milk and sugar without editing the base coffee.
benefits: Preserve the wrapped object and common interface.
decorator.when: Use it to layer combinable responsibilities at runtime.
decorator.avoid: Define rules before layering tightly coupled responsibilities or order-sensitive side effects.
decorator.tradeoff: Nested wrappers complicate debugging and identity checks. Order can affect behavior.
decorator.remember: Keep the interface and wrap new responsibilities around it.

decorator.principleTitle: Layer responsibilities without changing the interface
keyIdeas: A decorator preserves the wrapped interface, so callers retain the same capability.

decorator.distinction: Proxy controls access; Decorator adds responsibilities. Their shapes are similar but their intent differs.

facade.scenario: Startup must connect a database, start the cache and open a logger in order.
facade.request: Reuse startup from multiple entry points and add validation.
facade.problem: Every caller must know subsystem details and ordering; duplicated orchestration omits steps.
facade.solution: A startup facade exposes start and coordinates database, cache and logger internally. Callers express intent; subsystems remain independently accessible.
benefits: Callers depend on a small entry point.
Contain subsystem changes behind the facade.
facade.when: Use it when a common task coordinates several complex subsystems.
facade.avoid: Skip it for an already simple object. Do not turn the facade into a giant business layer.
facade.tradeoff: Split facades by task and handle failure and rollback explicitly.
facade.remember: Offer one simple entry point without removing the underlying structure.

flyweight.scenario: Many map trees duplicate species and color while their positions differ.
flyweight.request: Add more trees without duplicating identical species data.
flyweight.problem: Combining immutable type data with per-instance positions duplicates state as the count grows.
flyweight.solution: Store species and color as immutable intrinsic state in TreeType. A factory caches by the full intrinsic-state key; each Tree retains a type reference and its extrinsic position. The example verifies sharing rather than claiming measured memory savings.
benefits: Keep extrinsic state independent per instance.
flyweight.when: Use it for many instances with substantial safely shareable state and measured memory pressure.
flyweight.avoid: Skip it for few objects or frequently changing shared state.
flyweight.tradeoff: Split state carefully, manage cache lifetime and avoid mutable shared state.
flyweight.remember: Share the tree type, not each tree's position.

proxy.scenario: Creating a large image loads it immediately, even before preview is opened.
proxy.request: Load on first display and reuse the loaded image afterward.
proxy.problem: Direct construction fixes the loading time. Per-caller lazy-loading branches duplicate resource management.
proxy.solution: A proxy implements the same display interface and delays constructing the real image. First display loads it, later calls delegate to the retained object. Callers use the proxy as an image.
benefits: Reuse the created object for later calls.
Centralize access control at the object boundary.
proxy.when: Use it to control access through lazy loading, authorization, caching or remote boundaries.
proxy.avoid: Skip it for cheap access. A proxy cannot make remote failures disappear.
proxy.tradeoff: It can delay costs and errors and needs a cache lifetime. Proxies primarily control access; decorators add responsibilities.
proxy.remember: Keep the interface and let a proxy decide when to access the real object.
